title: Learning Loss: Urgent Crisis or Harmful Myth?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler engages the debate over the term learning loss, accepting that the pandemic left students behind, especially lower-income ones, and that schools must help them catch up. She rejects the radical critique that celebrates learning found, arguing that schools exist to introduce academic knowledge that some children get at home and others do not. She examines the slogan accelerate, don't remediate, granting that it fits elementary math, history, literature and science but not phonics or upper-level math, where foundations matter. Her sharpest point is that reading comprehension skills practice, whether remedial or accelerated, was already producing learning loss before the pandemic. She argues that tutoring built on that approach will repeat the failure and recommends rich content curricula, read-alouds and discussion instead.
points: Whatever it is called, the pandemic gap is real and schools should work to close it, though the right method depends on what kind of learning is at issue.
Celebrating learning found risks disadvantaging students, because schools exist to teach academic knowledge that some children cannot get at home.
Accelerate, don't remediate suits content subjects and elementary math but fails for systematic phonics and for upper-level math with missing foundations.
Practising isolated comprehension skills on easier or harder texts is the pre-pandemic failure, and widespread tutoring built on it will repeat the mistake.
The remedy is knowledge-rich curricula plus read-alouds and discussion for students who cannot yet read complex text independently.
quotes: The problem with K-12 education, according to this perspective, is that it hasn’t placed enough value on the knowledge students acquire from their families and communities. That’s not only disrespectful, some argue, it lowers teachers’ expectations and undermines students’ motivation.

But this philosophy can end up further disadvantaging the very students it aims to support. Institutions of higher learning and employers may aim for diversity, but they’re unlikely to start admitting applicants on the basis of how much they know about cooking, family traditions, or even racism.

While teachers should be respectful of the knowledge all kids bring with them, school is supposed to introduce students to new knowledge—primarily, academic knowledge. That’s the kind of knowledge some kids are able to pick up at home, while others—through no fault of their own—are not. There’s a lot more that schools can do to level the playing field for those two groups than they’ve done in the past.

That approach certainly seems to make sense in some contexts—for example, in elementary math, where one large-scale study has supported acceleration over remediation. It’s also probably the way to go in history, literature, or science.

But it probably won’t work with foundational reading skills like phonics. Students often need to learn letter-sound correspondences systematically rather than on an ad hoc “acceleration” basis. Many kids were getting ineffective ad hoc phonics instruction even before the pandemic because of defects in teacher preparation, leading to lasting reading problems.

Through elementary school and often beyond, schools spend many hours every week on the same round of “skills”—finding the main idea, making inferences, comparing and contrasting. The skills are the same every year, so “remediation” would mean having students practice the skills on easier texts—the same approach schools have been taking for decades, with dismal results.

So yes, let’s accelerate rather than remediate—but through curricula that focus on rich content rather than illusory comprehension skills, and through read-alouds and class discussion for students whose reading ability doesn’t yet allow them to access complex text on their own. And let’s acknowledge that schools can teach all kids valuable things, even if they haven’t done a great job of that in the past.
